name: Velorin
description: Velorin is a synaptic transmission accelerator that temporarily upregulates acetylcholine receptor density and increases axonal conduction velocity across motor pathways, shaving 30-60 milliseconds off average reaction time. Developed to allow unaugmented combatants to compete against chrome-heavy opponents, Velorin is Helix's flagship combat product and represents years of SNT-adjacent neuropharmacology research. The perceptual effect is often described as the world slowing slightly while the user's body moves at normal speed.
effects: Reaction time reduction of 30-60ms from individual baseline
Improved fine motor precision under stress
Subjective perception of slightly slowed external movement
Enhanced hand-eye coordination and target tracking
Mild elevation of processing speed for threat recognition
side_effects: Severe muscle tremors and fasciculations after drug clears
Acetylcholine rebound causing temporary weakness and coordination loss post-duration
Hypersensitivity to sensory input during peak effect — loud sounds and bright lights are painful
Risk of seizure if combined with BCI stimulation protocols
Chronic use degrades baseline reaction time as nervous system compensates
cultural_context: Velorin is the great equalizer — unaugmented fighters who can afford it can close the gap against lightly-chromed opponents. This creates a strange economic dynamic: chrome costs thousands of phi upfront, while Velorin costs hundreds per engagement. For runners who can't afford augmentation, Velorin is a subscription fee for staying competitive. There's a subculture of 'clean fighters' on the competitive circuit who use Velorin specifically because it doesn't qualify as augmentation under most underground fighting rules.
story_hooks: A Helix researcher approaches a runner with an offer: beta-test the next-generation Velorin formulation, which promises 80ms reduction, in exchange for combat field data — but the waiver they're asked to sign has unusual indemnity clauses.

Someone is manufacturing a street version of Velorin that has an 80% chance of working and a 20% chance of triggering a grand mal seizure — and the counterfeit packaging is indistinguishable from the real thing.

A Tier 2 fighter has been using Velorin daily for three years and now has slower baseline reflexes than someone who's never taken it — she needs the drug just to reach normal human speed, and Helix may have known this would happen.
